1_Abstract: Inverted (p–i–n) perovskite solar cells (PSCs) offer a promising pathway toward efficient and stable photovoltaics, yet interfacial and bulk defects limit their performance. This work significantly enhances device efficiency by evolving from conventional self-assembled monolayer (SAM) and additive engineering in the perovskite precursor—using MeO-4PADBC, PEAI, and PEABr—to a dual-strategy incorporating optimized bulk additives (py3, DMACPA, MACl, PMACl) followed by a targeted phenethylammonium chloride (PEACl) surface passivation treatment. The PEACl layer, applied via spin-coating and thermal annealing, induced the formation of a two-dimensional (2D) perovskite phase at the surface, evidenced by a distinct XRD peak at 4.00° with high intensity (71.75 cts), completely absent in the control device. This structural modification critically reduced residual tensile stress within the perovskite film by 53.3%, from 22.5 MPa to 10.5 MPa, as measured by grazing-incidence XRD, by accommodating lattice strain and passivating surface defects through the flexible organic-inorganic layered structure. Consequently, the optimized devices achieved a substantially enhanced power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 19.40%, representing a significant improvement over the control PCE of 16.79%. This performance gain stems directly from concurrent increases in open-circuit voltage (VOC) from 1.085 V to 1.104 V, fill factor (FF) from 66.45% to 73.62%, and short-circuit current density (JSC) from 23.29 mA/cm² to 23.87 mA/cm². The VOC and FF improvements are attributed to reduced non-radiative recombination losses via effective surface passivation, while the JSC increase reflects improved charge extraction. The synergistic reduction in film stress and defect density demonstrates that the PEACl-induced 2D/3D heterostructure simultaneously boosts optoelectronic properties and mechanical stability. This straightforward surface engineering approach provides a highly effective route to high-performance inverted PSCs, addressing key challenges in efficiency and operational stability for future commercialization.

2_Method.2_1_Control_F_P: Systematic parameter adjustments underlie the fabrication of a perovskite cell that was constituted, capturing how controlled conditions influence a PCE of 16.79%, FF of 66.45%, Voc of 1.08523 V, and Jsc of 23.29 mA/cm². The core perovskite solution, composed of Cs0.05MA0.16FA0.79Pb1I2.9Br0.1 at 1.73 mol/L, served as the foundational matrix for the solar cell. The SAM material MeO-4PADBC (0.33 mg/mL) was subsequently added into the perovskite solution to enhance interfacial properties and optimize device performance. The addition of PEAI (2 mg/mL) and PEABr (0.5 mg/mL) were then completed. The prepared precursor solution was spin-coated at 1000 rpm for 10 s and 5000 rpm for 30 s onto the substrate. In the last 6 s of the second step, the anti-solvent (160 µL of chlorobenzene) was dropped in the center at a constant rate The substrates were sequentially heated at 110 °C for 25 min for perovskite crystal formation. XRD analysis showed a diffraction peak was identified at around 12.65°, with an intensity of 755.1113203 cts and a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.247029369, which corresponds to the characteristic peak of PbI2. The relatively low intensity of this peak suggests a limited presence of residual PbI2. XRD analysis showed a diffraction peak was identified at 4.00°, with an intensity of 0.0 cts，which corresponds to the formation of a 2D structure within the perovskite lattice. The high intensity implies efficient surface passivation, contributing positively to device performance. GIXRD analysis further revealed a residual tensile stress of 22.5 MPa in the perovskite film via measurement conducted at an incident angle of 1°.
2_Method.2_2_Optimized_F_P: PSCs based on additives achieved a PCE of 19.4%, with a VOC of 1.10385 V, FF of 73.62%, and JSC of 23.87 mA/cm². A 1.73 mol/L Cs0.05MA0.16FA0.79Pb1I2.9Br0.1 precursor solution was similarly prepared using a mixture of DMF and DMSO. The py3 concentration is 1.0 mg/mL and DMACPA concentration is 3.0 mg/mL. MACl (7 mg/mL) and PMACl (0.7 mg/mL) were incorporated as additives. Then, the perovskite precursor solution was spin-coated at 1000 rpm for 15 s, and then at 5000 rpm for 30 s. A timed antisolvent drop (180 µL at last 10 s) enhanced the perovskite crystallization kinetics. The film was immediately annealed at 105 °C for 30 min. PEACl (1.6 mg/mL) was spin-coated onto the sample surface to serve as a passivation layer, thereby improving device performance. And then it was spin-coated on the cooled perovskite films at 4900.0 rpm for 35.0 s. At a timing of 17.0 s, 120.0 µL of passivator was introduced into the spinning passivation layer. And then transferred to the hotplate and annealed at 110.0 ℃ for 5.0 min. XRD analysis showed a diffraction peak was identified at 4.00°, with an intensity of 71.74596607 cts，which corresponds to the formation of a 2D structure within the perovskite lattice. The high intensity implies efficient surface passivation, contributing positively to device performance. GIXRD analysis further revealed a residual tensile stress of 10.5 MPa in the perovskite film via measurement conducted at an incident angle of 1°.

3_Result_Discussion:
# Analysis of PEACl Surface Treatment Effects on Perovskite XRD Characteristics

## Peak Intensity at ~4°
When comparing the control device (without PEACl treatment) to the target device (with PEACl surface treatment), there is a dramatic change in the low-dimensional perovskite characteristic peak at 4.00°:

- **Control device**: Peak intensity = 0.0 cts (completely absent)
- **Target device**: Peak intensity = 71.74596607 cts

This represents a significant transformation - the PEACl surface treatment has induced the formation of a distinct low-dimensional (2D) perovskite structure at the surface that was completely absent in the control device. The appearance of this peak is direct evidence of successful surface engineering where the bulky phenethylammonium (PEA+) cations from PEACl have intercalated at the perovskite surface/grain boundaries, forming a 2D Ruddlesden-Popper phase.

## Residual Stress Changes
The GIXRD analysis reveals important mechanical changes:

- **Control device**: Residual tensile stress = 22.5 MPa
- **Target device**: Residual tensile stress = 10.5 MPa

This represents a **53.3% reduction** in tensile stress (from 22.5 MPa to 10.5 MPa) following PEACl surface treatment.

## Scientific Explanation
The formation of the 2D perovskite phase at the surface (evidenced by the new 4° peak) directly contributes to stress relaxation in the film. The bulky organic cations in the 2D structure:

1. Create a more flexible organic-inorganic layered structure at the surface
2. Accommodate lattice mismatch between grains
3. Reduce strain propagation through the film
4. Passivate surface defects that can act as stress concentration points

This stress reduction is critically important for device stability, as high residual tensile stress is a major contributor to perovskite film degradation and failure mechanisms. The simultaneous appearance of the 4° peak and stress reduction confirms the successful formation of a passivating 2D layer that both improves electronic properties (as evidenced by the PCE increase from 16.79% to 19.4%) and enhances mechanical stability.

The XRD data provides direct structural evidence that PEACl surface treatment effectively creates a beneficial 2D/3D heterostructure that improves both the optoelectronic and mechanical properties of the perovskite solar cell.
